Minor Scales and Key Signatures: From La

Chapter 3 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom for students who already read and write in minor with la-based movable do: natural, harmonic and melodic minor, relative and parallel keys, and minor key signatures as names for what they already audiate.

This page goes with Chapter 3, Minor Scales and Key Signatures of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom.

You already know this. You sing in minor with la as the resting tone (movable do, la-based minor; Gordon 105), you sing harmonic minor with the raised si (Gordon 70), and you read both from the do signature. This chapter names what you already do. La-based minor gives you a head start: the book’s “relative minor” is the minor you’ve always sung.

Press ▶ to hear an example, or ▶ Sing to hear it sung on syllables. Click any heading to fold its section.

What you know → what the book calls it

You say (MLT) The book says (Hutchinson ch. 3)
la, the resting tone in minor tonic of the minor key, 1̂
la ti do re mi fa so la natural minor scale (Gordon: Aeolian tonality)
the same notes with si for so harmonic minor scale (Gordon: harmonic minor tonality)
the do signature, resting on la the minor key signature: “A minor”
major and minor with the same do signature relative keys
the same tonic letter, major and minor parallel keys

3.1 Three kinds of minor

Read 3.1

Natural minor is la to la with no changes, the notes of the do signature from la. You’ve sung it as the minor of folk tunes and of Gordon’s Aeolian tonality.

Harmonic minor raises so to si, so the scale has a half step into la like the half step ti–do in major. That’s the dominant sound you sing in harmonic minor patterns such as mi si ti re (Gordon 100). The book shows it as an accidental: in A minor, G becomes G♯.

Melodic minor raises both fa and so on the way up, and goes back to natural minor on the way down. This one may be new: you have the sound of si, but probably not of the raised fa. In movable do, raised fa is usually sung fi (the syllable is common practice, not yet checked against an MLT source).

Where the book and MLT differ. The book treats natural, harmonic and melodic minor as three forms of one minor key. Gordon treats harmonic minor and Aeolian as two different tonalities, each with its own characteristic patterns (Gordon 149). Both see the same notes; Gordon names what you hear, the book names what is written.

3.2 Minor key signatures: the same do signature

Read 3.2

You already read a do signature and rest on la. The book calls that key “the relative minor”:

  • Find do, then go down to la (two letters down, or up six). One sharp: do is G, la is E → E minor. Three flats: do is E♭, la is C → C minor.
  • Relative keys share a signature: C major and A minor, G major and E minor. In MLT terms they share a do signature, with different resting tones (Gordon 155–156).
  • Parallel keys share a tonic letter: A major and A minor. In MLT terms, do moves: A major has do on A; A minor has la on A, so do is on C.

The same tune, on the same do signature, ends on do (major) or la (minor):

The harmonic minor accidental isn’t in the signature. Si is always written in the music. That’s why C minor’s signature is three flats, but its scale needs a B♮.

Practise: name the minor key

3.3 Scale degree names in minor

Read 3.3

The book numbers minor from its own tonic, so la is 1̂. The names are the ones from major, with one change: so (a whole step below la) is the subtonic, and si (a half step below) is the leading tone, as ti is in major.

Syllable Degree Name
la 1̂ tonic
ti 2̂ supertonic
do 3̂ mediant
re 4̂ subdominant
mi 5̂ dominant
fa 6̂ submediant
so / si 7̂ subtonic / leading tone

So “the dominant” in minor is mi, the note your harmonic minor dominant patterns start on.

Bridging: from la to the book’s names

  1. Find do, then la. Say both letters: “do is B♭, la is G: G minor.”
  2. Sing la to la, then again on letters. That’s natural minor.
  3. Swap in si: raise the letter under so with a sharp or natural. That’s harmonic minor.
  4. Parallel key? Keep the tonic letter, move do: G major has do on G (one sharp); G minor has la on G (do on B♭, two flats).

Check yourself

  1. Two sharps. What is the relative minor?
  2. In D minor, what letter is si?
  3. In E minor harmonic, which note gets an accidental?
  4. What is the parallel minor of E♭ major, and its signature?
  5. In minor, which syllable is the dominant, 5̂?
TipAnswers
  1. B minor (do is D, la is B).
  2. C♯.
  3. D becomes D♯ (so → si).
  4. E♭ minor, six flats (la on E♭, so do is on G♭).
  5. Mi.

All the key-signature drills are on Theory Drills. Related: Modes: Three Meanings of One Word. Next: Rhythm Notation from Du De.
